title: Lectio in the cloister
hook: reading slowly, chewing words like a cow chews cud

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cellarer, and tools as altar vessels. Your line was every pot is holy. What did you wash or put away as if it belonged in church? Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

Idleness is the enemy of the soul. That's how Benedict opens his chapter on the daily work. But he doesn't fill every hour with labor. He splits the day between work with the hands and holy reading. Lectio divina, he calls it. And in the long season of Lent, each monk is handed a book from the library, to read through from start to finish. Then, the Rule says, a senior monk or two should go round the monastery during the reading hours, to make sure nobody's idling or chatting instead of reading. Picture a quiet covered walkway, monks on benches with books open, and someone strolling past to keep them honest. Today's word: lectio in the cloister.

Lectio means reading. But not the kind you do on a phone, scrolling for the next thing. Some monastic writers reached for a farmyard picture: a cow chewing the cud. The cow eats, rests, brings it back up, and chews again, getting everything out of it. A Carthusian monk named Guigo set out four steps. Reading puts the food in your mouth. Meditation chews it and breaks it down. Prayer tastes it. And contemplation is the sweetness itself. You go slowly enough to taste. The Bible already talks about words this way. A psalm says, "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" Ezekiel is handed a scroll and told to eat it, and he says, "Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." Eating, tasting, honey. Words you take in and digest, not just pass your eyes over. And the very first psalm describes the blessed man as the one whose "delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." Day and night is a long time to chew one thing. That's the point. Lectio isn't about how much you read. It's how long you stay with a little. One verse, turned over and over, until something in it opens. And pairing it with work does something. The chewing carries on. The verse from the morning reading goes out to the garden, and comes back up between rows of beans. The cloister's just where it starts.

Here's the practice: chew one verse all day. Here's one, from the psalm we just heard: how sweet are thy words unto my taste. Say it once, slowly, under your breath. Then again, and lean on a different word: how sweet. Thy words. Unto my taste. Notice which word catches. Stay with that one. When your mind drifts, come back to the verse. If you'd rather choose another line you love, do. The bell holds the time.
Lectio in the cloister. Holy reading, done slowly, in the monastery's quiet walkway, words chewed and tasted rather than skimmed.
Your line: chew it slowly. Take your verse with you today. Bring it back up three times, at a sink, on a walk, waiting in line, and chew again. Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns set aside daily time for lectio divina, slow prayerful reading of scripture, and lay Christians, Catholic and Protestant, also practice it by reading a short passage several times and staying with a word or phrase.

original.note: Latin, from Rule chapter forty-eight: holy reading.

trapdoor: what you thought: lectio is just reading the Bible.
what it means: slow reading, chewed and tasted, and carried into the work of the day.
what a scholar hears: Guigo's four steps, reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation, give the cud-chewing picture a shape.

notes: Rule 48 paraphrased: 'otiositas inimica est animae'; set times for manual labor and for lectio divina; in Lent each receives a book from the library to read through in order and entirely; one or two seniors go round at reading times to see no one is idle or chatting. Confirm.
The cud-chewing (ruminatio) picture is attributed loosely to 'monastic writers'; it is not in Rule 48. Confirm attribution is fair.

Guigo II's Ladder of Monks is paraphrased (reading puts food in the mouth, meditation chews it, prayer tastes, contemplation is the sweetness). Check wording, especially the assignment of 'tastes' and 'sweetness'. No date is given.
'The very first psalm' refers to Psalm 1 by its position, which the citation states.
howItsDone says lay Catholics and Protestants also practice lectio; a general description, no count claimed.

Editor pass: Guigo's steps are no longer called rungs or a ladder (day 1116 just used the ladder image); 'happy' changed to the KJV's 'blessed'; 'monastic writers' softened to 'some'; the reason Benedict pairs reading with work is no longer put in his mouth; 'in a line' clarified so it isn't heard as 'your line'.

Audit pass: Rule 48 has one or two seniors go round the monastery (circumeant monasterium) looking for a brother idle or chatting; the script had them walk the cloister looking for dozers, so the hook, myth and fork reveal now follow the Rule (the cloister picture is kept as a picture). Guigo identified as a Carthusian; Psalm 119:103, Ezekiel 3:3, Psalm 1:2 exact KJV.
